title: Parallel Tool Calls and Streaming with Tools

questions.question: Three independent weather lookups take 400, 600, and 800 ms. Ignoring overhead, how long should concurrent execution take?
options: About 600 ms, because the middle call sets the wall time
About 800 ms, because the slowest call sets the wall time
About 2,400 ms, because concurrency multiplies each delay
About 1,800 ms, because every call must finish in sequence
questions.explanation: Independent calls overlap, so ideal concurrent wall time is max(400, 600, 800)=800 ms, ignoring setup overhead. The 1,800 ms alternative sums the delays and describes sequential execution; the middle call does not determine when the slowest call finishes.

questions.question: A workflow must create a file and then write its contents. What is the safest parallel-call choice?
options: Run both calls together and sort results by completion time
Disable parallelism because the second action depends on the first
Enable parallelism because both actions use the same host
Stream both argument objects and execute each partial prefix
questions.explanation: Writing depends on the file-creation result, so concurrent launch can reach write_file before the file exists. Disable parallelism or model the dependency explicitly; sorting results afterward cannot undo an action that ran too early.

questions.question: Calls complete in unpredictable order. What must the host preserve when returning results?
options: The same completion order as the model's request list
The matching call id on each individual tool result
A shared result string that merges all call outputs
The original tool-list position without any identifier
questions.explanation: Each result must echo its call id so the host and model can match it to the request regardless of completion order. Request-list order is not a reliable identifier when a call is delayed, dropped, duplicated, or two calls share a name.

questions.question: A streamed tool call has only supplied part of its JSON arguments. When should the host parse the accumulated string?
options: After the provider signals that the call is complete
As soon as the first opening brace arrives
Before storing the first delta chunk by call index
After counting matching braces in the partial buffer
questions.explanation: Accumulate argument fragments for that call and parse only after the provider signals completion. A matching-brace count can be fooled by braces inside quoted or escaped strings, so the partial buffer is not yet trustworthy JSON.

questions.question: Three argument streams interleave for calls A, B, and C. How should the accumulator organize fragments?
options: Store fragments by tool name and overwrite earlier calls
Create a buffer only after the final call stops
Append every fragment to one shared JSON string
Keep a separate buffer for each call id or call index
questions.explanation: Maintain one argument buffer per call id or provider index, appending each arriving chunk to its own call. A shared string or a buffer keyed only by tool name mixes the three get_weather payloads together.

questions.question: A downstream API cannot handle a wide fan-out without rate-limit failures. Which design response matches the lesson?
options: Increase the worker pool until every call starts immediately
Retry all failed calls concurrently without a per-call cap
Parse streaming arguments earlier to reduce executor latency
Disable or limit parallel fan-out to fit downstream capacity
questions.explanation: Cap concurrency or disable fan-out when the downstream service is rate-limited; a wide burst can exceed its capacity even if the client supports parallel calls. Increasing workers or retrying everything at once compounds the same load.
